category: Application framework, editions and licensing, library services, EDAi and file types
description: The Proteus application shell (Home page, module tabs, install modes, themes, docking, samples, updates), the licensing models and product editions (Starter Kit through Level 3, Platinum, Enterprise, Custom, VSM/Visual Designer add-ons, educational schemes), the library services shared by schematic and PCB (web search import, Import Part, managed libraries with Git/SVN, BSDL import, AI Library Parts), the EDAi assistants, and the project/library/model file types (.pdsprj, .pdsbak, .pdsclip, .SEC, .MDF, .LIB/.IDX, .SDF).

tools.name: Home page (Proteus application shell)
tools.description: The start tab of PDS.EXE: New Project wizard, Open Project, Open Sample (filterable sample library incl. the Tutorials category), recent projects, the News panel with update notices and download links (software updates are delivered through it under the Update Service Contract), licence status and the version number at the bottom-left. Every module opens as a tab beside it.
tools.usage: Launch Proteus > Home tab > New Project / Open Project / Open Sample / News panel; Help menu for module help files
tools.example: Home > Open Sample > category Tutorials > 'dsPIC33 Recorder (schematic only)' to follow the Getting Started PCB guide.
tools.notes: The version shown here tells you whether a feature (e.g. Push routing 8.16, MicroPython 8.17 SP4) is available.

tools.name: Module tabs (Schematic Capture, PCB Layout, 3D Viewer, Gerber Viewer, Source Code, Design Explorer, Visual Designer, BOM, Project Notes, Library Manager)
tools.description: Proteus is one application with modules opened as tabs from the module toolbar; any tab can be dragged out of the frame to create an additional window for side-by-side work (schematic + BOM, layout + 3D Viewer, schematic + Source Code on two monitors). All modules share the single project database, so a wiring change appears in the layout ratsnest, the BOM and the 3D view live.
tools.usage: Module toolbar icons at the top of the window > open the tab; drag a tab title out of the frame to undock it; drag back to redock
tools.example: Drag the VSM Studio tab to the second monitor so the schematic animates while stepping code.
tools.notes: Some modules need licences (3D Viewer: Level 2+; Visual Designer/IoT Builder: their products).

tools.name: Install modes (all users, single user, portable)
tools.description: Proteus 9 installs in one of three modes: for all users of the PC, for the current user only, or portable (self-contained folder that can be carried between machines, e.g. on a USB drive) - chosen in the installer and reflected in where settings, libraries and licence data are kept. Registry licence keys, USB dongles and server/cloud licences all work with these modes.
tools.usage: Installer > choose All Users / Single User / Portable; settings paths follow the mode (see System Settings)
tools.example: A portable install on a lab USB stick lets a cloud-licensed student run the same setup on any classroom PC.
tools.notes: Proteus 9 is a native 64-bit application with Unicode (UTF-8) support; Proteus 8 was 32-bit.

tools.name: Light and dark theme
tools.description: Proteus 9's framework supports a light and a dark UI theme, following the Windows theme preference by default and switchable in the application; dialogues, object selectors and toolbars were redesigned for both. Schematic/PCB colours remain governed by the design template (Template > Set Design Defaults), so a dark UI does not alter printed output.
tools.usage: System / application settings > Theme: Light / Dark / Follow Windows
tools.example: Dark theme for the UI with a white-paper template so PDF exports still print correctly.
tools.notes: Available from Proteus 9.0.

tools.name: Dockable widgets (live DRC, CRC, instruments)
tools.description: In Proteus 9 the popup windows for the live Design Rule Checker, the Connectivity Rule Checker, instruments (System Scope, meters) and similar tools behave as dock widgets that can be pinned to the bottom or sides of the frame or floated, and icon groups/sizes can be adjusted to free editor space. The status bar keeps a message history.
tools.usage: Open the DRC/CRC list or an instrument > drag its title to a dock area or float it; icon grouping options in the toolbar settings
tools.example: Dock the DRC violation list under the layout and click entries to zoom to each problem while routing.
tools.notes: Proteus 8 used floating popups instead.

tools.name: Open Sample (sample projects library)
tools.description: A categorised library of ready-made projects installed with Proteus - tutorials (schematic, PCB, simulation, VSM Studio stages), per-family microcontroller examples (PIC, AVR, Arduino, 8051, ARM, MSP430, MicroPython), Visual Designer/IoT Builder projects, analogue/digital simulation demonstrations and PCB examples - opened from the Home page with a keyword/category filter. They are the fastest way to see how a peripheral or instrument is wired.
tools.usage: Home > Open Sample > filter by category/keyword > double-click the project (opens a copy)

parameters.name: Category
parameters.description: Tutorials, VSM family folders, PCB, Visual Designer, etc.

tools.example: Open Sample > 'Analogue Simulation Tutorial (Part 2)' to load the op-amp circuit used in the graph-based analysis guide.
tools.notes: Samples are also listed on the Labcenter website's sample projects page.

tools.name: Update Service Contract (USC) and software updates
tools.description: Labcenter's maintenance scheme: a new licence includes 6 months of USC (3 months for module additions/upgrades), renewable for 1-3 years per licence, and all releases - including major versions such as 8.x to 9 - are delivered under it, typically a feature release every six months plus maintenance builds. When USC lapses the installed version keeps working but new releases cannot be downloaded; updates appear in the Home page News panel and the current version is shown bottom-left.
tools.usage: Home page News panel > update notice > download; renewal offers appear on the Home page for current software
tools.example: A 8.15 licence with expired USC can install 8.15 SP builds only; renewing USC unlocks 8.17 and 9.x downloads.
tools.notes: Support email remains available regardless of USC; older versions get reduced support.

tools.name: Licence types (registry key, USB dongle, network licence server, cloud licence)
tools.description: Proteus licences are delivered as registry-based licence keys (single PC), USB hardware dongles (movable between machines), server-based network licences (a licence server with a USB dongle serving floating seats on one LAN subnet with automatic compliance) and cloud licences for enterprise/education (session licensed via URL, managed in the Labcenter web portal with seat allocation, credentials, reservations, access logs, heartbeat monitoring and authorised IP lists - 8.11/8.12). The Licence Manager utility installs and inspects keys on a workstation.
tools.usage: Help > About / Licence Manager to install a key file or activate; network: install the licence server on a LAN host and point clients to it; cloud: log in from the client with portal credentials
tools.example: A university buys a 50-seat cloud licence; the lecturer creates groups in the portal and reserves 30 seats for Tuesday's lab.
tools.notes: Network use is limited to a single LAN subnet; cloud licensing lets students use the full package from home.

tools.name: PCB Design Starter Kit (500 pins)
tools.description: The entry-level edition: schematic capture and PCB layout limited to 500 pins per design, with the standard feature set (layer stackup, design rules, basic power planes, shape-based autorouter in automatic mode, Gerber X2/RS274X output) and basic SPICE simulation; the Advanced Simulation Features module can be added to it. Suitable for small boards and learning.
tools.usage: Pricing > PCB Design Starter Kit; upgrade later by paying the difference (100% credit)
tools.example: An Arduino shield with two ICs and connectors fits comfortably under 500 pins.
tools.notes: Pin count includes every pin of every placed component, not just connected pins.

tools.name: PCB Design Level 1 and Level 1+ (1000 / 2000 pins)
tools.description: Standard-feature-set editions with higher capacity: Level 1 allows 1000 pins and Level 1+ 2000 pins per design. They include the integrated shape-based autorouter and basic simulation but not the professional features (3D Viewer, MCAD export, differential pairs, length matching, unlimited polygonal planes, scriptable routing, autoplacement, dynamic teardrops).
tools.usage: Pricing > PCB Design Level 1 / Level 1+
tools.example: A 64-pin MCU board with a dozen peripherals typically lands around 600-900 pins - Level 1 territory.
tools.notes: Upgrading to Level 2 adds the professional feature set at the same pin count.

tools.name: PCB Design Level 2 and Level 2+ (Professional feature set)
tools.description: The first editions with the Advanced/Professional feature set - 3D Viewer with STEP/IGES/STL/IDF export, differential pair routing with skew correction, automatic length matching and match groups, unlimited polygonal power planes per layer, scriptable/interactive autorouting, board autoplacement with rooms, dynamic teardrops and tapers, HDI micro-vias, ODB++ output - at 1000 pins (Level 2) or 2000 pins (Level 2+).
tools.usage: Pricing > PCB Design Level 2 / Level 2+
tools.example: A USB 2.0 device board needing diff-pair routing and a 3D fit check needs Level 2 even though it is under 1000 pins.
tools.notes: Feature descriptions marked 'Level 2 or higher' throughout the documentation refer to this set.

tools.name: PCB Design Level 3 (unlimited pins)
tools.description: The top stand-alone PCB edition: the complete professional feature set with no design-capacity limit, used for large multi-layer boards and multi-board products. It is the PCB component of the Enterprise and Platinum packages.
tools.usage: Pricing > PCB Design Level 3
tools.example: A 6-layer FPGA carrier with 1500-pin BGA and DDR needs Level 3 for capacity and Level 2+ features.
tools.notes: Simulation families are separate licences unless bought in Enterprise/Platinum.

tools.name: Proteus Platinum Edition
tools.description: 'Includes absolutely everything that we sell': unlimited PCB Design (Level 3 features), ProSPICE with Advanced Simulation Features, every VSM microcontroller family (over 750 processor models: PIC10-dsPIC33, AVR/Arduino, 8051, ARM7/Cortex-M0/M3/M4, MSP430/Piccolo, MicroPython), USB Simulation Support, all embedded peripheral libraries, Visual Designer for Arduino, Raspberry Pi and MicroPython, and IoT Builder.
tools.usage: Pricing > Platinum
tools.example: A training centre teaching every MCU family and PCB design buys Platinum rather than composing a Custom package.
tools.notes: Enterprise is the commercial-PCB equivalent without the Visual Designer/IoT Builder modules.

tools.name: Proteus Enterprise Edition
tools.description: The commercial product-design package: unlimited professional PCB layout, high-speed design (differential pairs, length matching), shape-based autorouter, library web access, ProSPICE with Advanced Simulation Features, all VSM microcontroller families, USB simulation and all peripheral libraries - i.e. everything needed from capture through simulation to manufacture, minus the educational-oriented Visual Designer and IoT Builder modules.
tools.usage: Pricing > Enterprise (also available as Enterprise Custom to pick modules)
tools.example: A product company standardising on Proteus for hardware and firmware teams licenses Enterprise with network licensing.
tools.notes: Enterprise cloud licensing adds the web portal with access logs and IP allow-lists.

tools.name: Custom package (modular configuration)
tools.description: The Package Configurator builds a licence from modules: a PCB Design level (Starter to Level 3), Advanced Simulation Features, any set of VSM families (individual families, bundles or starter kits), Visual Designer products (Arduino, Raspberry Pi, MicroPython or bundle) and IoT Builder, at lower cost than Platinum and upgradeable later with full credit for the previous purchase.
tools.usage: Pricing > Package Configurator > pick PCB level, simulation, VSM families, Visual Designer, IoT Builder > quotation
tools.example: Level 2 + Advanced Simulation + PIC 8-bit bundle + AVR for a mixed PIC/Arduino product line.
tools.notes: Additional licences at the same or lower level get a 30% discount.

tools.name: Visual Designer product editions (Arduino, Raspberry Pi, MicroPython, bundle)
tools.description: Visual Designer is sold per target ecosystem - Visual Designer for Arduino (AVR Arduinos, STM32 Blue Pill, Robot Turtles), for Raspberry Pi and for MicroPython (Pico/ESP32/Pyboard, 9.1) - or as a bundle of all three; each includes the flowchart editor, peripheral gallery, simulation and hardware deployment for its targets, and IoT Builder is an add-on to any of them. Educational variants exist for classroom use.
tools.usage: Pricing > Visual Designer > Arduino / Raspberry Pi / MicroPython / Bundle; add IoT Builder
tools.example: A school buys Visual Designer for Arduino + IoT Builder for a connected-devices course.
tools.notes: The underlying VSM processor licence for the target family is included with the Visual Designer product.

tools.name: Educational licensing (EDU pricing, classroom and cloud licences, student licences, ProTutor)
tools.description: Education-specific terms: single-user educational licences at 20% below commercial price, multi-user classroom discounts (10, 25, 50, 100, 200+ seats), locally installed, server-based or cloud licensing, and student home-use licences while the institution's software is under maintenance. Cloud licensing lets lecturers create groups, credentials and calendar reservations in the portal; ProTutor is the education edition of the EDAi assistant.
tools.usage: Pricing > Education > choose licence scheme and seat count; cloud portal for group/reservation management
tools.example: 50-seat cloud licence with a reserved block for lab hours and free-pool access for evening homework.
tools.notes: An online quotation wizard produces an instant single-user quote.

tools.name: EDAi ProPilot (AI design assistant)
tools.description: Introduced in Proteus 9.1 for commercial users: an AI assistant inside Proteus that helps design analogue/digital circuits and validate signals, answers help questions through retrieval over the Proteus documentation, generates peripheral set-up code for embedded projects and, from 9.2, interprets simulation results (automated probe placement, extracting cut-off frequencies, quantifying power-rail ripple).
tools.usage: EDAi pane/ProPilot tab > ask a design, help or coding question; accept generated code into the Source Code project
tools.example: Ask ProPilot for the I2C initialisation code for an MCP23017 on a PIC18F46K22 and paste it into main.c; then ask it to place probes and report the 3dB point of the filter graph.
tools.notes: Requires an EDAi subscription; ProTutor is the educational counterpart.

tools.name: EDAi ProTutor (AI for education)
tools.description: The educational version of the EDAi assistant (9.1) aimed at students and teachers: explains circuits and simulation results, guides through Proteus features with documentation-backed answers and supports coding help in a tutoring style rather than delivering finished designs.
tools.usage: EDAi pane > ProTutor (education licences)
tools.example: A student asks why the RC filter output lags the input and ProTutor explains phase shift with reference to the Frequency graph.
tools.notes: Availability is tied to educational licences.

tools.name: AI Library Parts (EDAi, beta)
tools.description: Proteus 9.2 beta feature of EDAi ProPilot: creates complete library parts (schematic symbol with pins, footprint and properties) from a natural-language description and datasheet pages, after first searching the installed and web libraries for an existing part, reducing manual Make Device/Make Package work for parts no vendor library carries.
tools.usage: EDAi > Library part generation > describe the part / attach datasheet pages > review the generated symbol and footprint > save to a user library
tools.example: 'Create a part for the XYZ123 sensor, 8-pin DFN 3x3mm, pins per page 4 of the attached datasheet' - review pad dimensions before use.
tools.notes: Beta: verify pin mapping and footprint dimensions against the datasheet before manufacturing.

tools.name: Library web search import (Pick Devices web results: SamacSys / Component Search Engine, SnapEDA)
tools.description: Since 8.9 the Pick Devices dialogue searches online part libraries as well as installed ones: switch from installed to web results with one button, and a double-click downloads and imports the schematic symbol, PCB footprint and (usually) 3D STEP model, placing the part in the user library and the current project. Over 15 million parts are available via SamacSys/Component Search Engine and (from 8.12) SnapEDA; missing parts can be requested and are typically built in 24-48 hours. A free SamacSys account is created from inside Proteus on first use.
tools.usage: Component Mode > P > Keywords > 'Web' results button > double-click a result > review parse log/previews > part appears in the object selector

parameters.name: Target library
parameters.description: User library that receives the imported part.

tools.example: Search 'LTC3588' > web results > double-click: symbol, MSOP-10 footprint and STEP model import in one step.
tools.notes: Imported parts have no simulation model; add SPICEMODEL/SPICEFILE if simulation is needed. Check pin mapping in the preview before placing.

tools.name: Library > Import Part (universal part importer)
tools.description: The importer for part packages downloaded manually from third-party vendors - SamacSys/Library Loader, SnapEDA, Ultra Librarian, PCB Library Expert and Digi-Key formats (8.8) - typically as a ZIP: it parses the vendor files, shows a parse log and previews, applies configuration settings if needed, then runs the footprint and component wizards so the part lands in a chosen library with description and categories. It is the offline counterpart of the web search import.
tools.usage: Library > Import Part > choose the downloaded ZIP or extracted folder (.p file for SamacSys) > review parse log and previews > Import footprint then component via the wizards

parameters.name: Source format
parameters.description: Vendor package type detected from the files.

tools.example: Download an Ultra Librarian ZIP for a connector, extract, Library > Import Part, accept the previews, and pick it from the user library.
tools.notes: BSDL scripts from the manufacturer can drive large FPGA/BGA part creation instead.

tools.name: Managed Libraries (librarian-approved parts with Git/SVN versioning)
tools.description: Proteus 9.0 introduced a managed-libraries workflow for design teams: usage can be restricted to librarian-approved, version-controlled library sets, with auditing tools that verify a design uses the latest component versions and pre-production checks that flag unmanaged parts; 9.1 added integrated Git and Subversion repository support so library history and status are visible inside the Library Manager. Library part properties can be edited in a spreadsheet view integrated with the Manage Changes dialogue (8.13).
tools.usage: Library Manager > configure the managed library set and repository (Git/SVN); System Settings > restrict picking to managed libraries; audit tools report out-of-date parts

parameters.name: Repository
parameters.description: Git or Subversion location of the managed libraries.

parameters.name: Restriction
parameters.description: Whether unmanaged parts may be picked.

tools.example: Librarian releases R0402_1k v2 with a corrected stock code; the audit flags every open design still on v1 and Manage Changes updates them.
tools.notes: Managed libraries are listed as a Library Manager module capability; the Library Manager was rewritten in 8.7 with previews and a part-differencing tool.

tools.name: BSDL and FPGA pinout import (Make Device for large BGAs)
tools.description: For high-pin-count FPGAs and BGAs the Make Device wizard can read a manufacturer BSDL file or an Altera/Xilinx pinout file to create the schematic part (multi-element symbols with pin names/numbers) automatically, and generic FPGA packaging tools generate the BGA footprint, so thousand-pin parts do not have to be drawn by hand. Introduced with the improved BGA workflow of 8.5.
tools.usage: Library > Make Device > import pins from BSDL / pinout file > split into elements > package with the BGA generator > save

parameters.name: BSDL / pinout file
parameters.description: Vendor description of pin names and numbers.

tools.example: Import the BSDL for an Artix-7 FBG484, split banks into separate symbol elements and attach a generated 484-ball footprint.
tools.notes: The library web search often already has the FPGA part; check there first.

tools.name: .pdsprj (Proteus project file)
tools.description: The single compound file that holds a Proteus 8/9 project: schematic sheets, PCB layout(s) including multi-board data, the shared project database, firmware project references (or embedded source/debug files with Embed Files), simulation and graph settings, design notes, BOM configuration and assembly variants. It is registered to PDS.EXE so double-clicking opens it, and it can be passed on the command line.
tools.usage: File > Save Project / Save Project As; PDS.EXE "path\project.pdsprj" opens it
tools.example: Archive a release by copying project.pdsprj plus any external firmware folder (or enable Embed Files first).
tools.notes: Proteus 8.15 changed the file format (not backwards compatible with earlier 8.x); Proteus 9 reads 8.x projects but 8.x cannot open 9 files.

tools.name: .pdsbak (project backup file)
tools.description: Automatic backup copy of the project written by the autosave/backup mechanism (interval and number of copies set in System Settings), named after the project with the .pdsbak extension in the project folder. To recover, rename or copy it to .pdsprj and open it in Proteus.
tools.usage: Recovery: copy project.pdsbak to project_recovered.pdsprj > File > Open Project
tools.example: After a crash, the .pdsbak from ten minutes earlier is renamed and opened to recover the layout.
tools.notes: Backups accumulate; clean old ones from the project folder periodically.

tools.name: .pdsclip (Project Clip / design snippet file)
tools.description: A saved section of schematic together with its corresponding PCB layout (routing, placement, rules) exported as a Project Clip for formal design re-use: import it into another project and both the circuit and its laid-out copper arrive intact. Clips live in the Project Clips directory set in System Settings and are also called design snippets in Labcenter literature.
tools.usage: Schematic: select the block > File > Export Project Clip (.pdsclip); File > Import Project Clip in the target project, then place on the sheet and the layout
tools.example: Save the USB-C power-delivery front end as USBPD.pdsclip and drop it into the next three products.
tools.notes: Annotation of imported parts is resolved by the Global Annotator; net names may need renaming to avoid merges.

tools.name: .SEC (section file: Export Section / Import Section)
tools.description: The older schematic-only re-use format: a tagged section of a sheet exported to a .SEC file and read into another design with Import Section, placing the objects at the cursor. It carries components, wires and graphics but not PCB data, for which Project Clips (.pdsclip) are preferred.
tools.usage: Tag the objects > File > Export Section > name.SEC; File > Import Section in another design > click to place
tools.example: Export a standard power-terminal/decoupling block as PWR.SEC and import it onto every new sheet.
tools.notes: Section files predate Proteus 8 and remain supported for legacy libraries of circuit fragments.

tools.name: .MDF (Model Definition File)
tools.description: Compiled simulator model produced by Tools > Model Compiler from a subcircuit sheet, or shipped by Labcenter in the MODELS directory (e.g. BIPOLAR.MDF, OPAMP.MDF, 74LS.MDF); a library part references it through the MODFILE property and the netlister expands it in place at simulation time with the part's properties substituted. The models path in System Settings must include its folder.
tools.usage: Tools > Model Compiler > output.MDF; device property MODFILE=output.MDF
tools.example: 'Cannot find model file bipolar.mdf' after moving an install: add the MODELS folder to the models path.
tools.notes: Distinct from .DLL (VSM SDK models) and .LIB (SPICE model libraries).

tools.name: .LIB / .IDX (Proteus library and index files)
tools.description: Proteus libraries are .LIB files holding schematic devices, PCB packages, symbols and 2D graphics, each paired with an .IDX index that makes the contents searchable in Pick Devices; installed libraries live in the LIBRARY directory and user libraries (USERDVC.LIB, USERPKG.LIB and any created in the Library Manager) in the user library path. Library paths are set in System Settings, and the Library Manager copies, moves, compares and deletes parts across .LIB files.
tools.usage: System Settings > library paths; Library Manager > create/copy/delete parts between .LIB files; Make Device/Make Package > choose the destination .LIB
tools.example: Create ACME_PARTS.LIB in the Library Manager and target it from Make Device so company parts stay separate from Labcenter's.
tools.notes: Note that SPICE model libraries (.LIB text files with .MODEL/.SUBCKT) are a different thing and are referenced via SPICEFILE/SPICELIB.

tools.name: .SDF (simulator netlist file)
tools.description: The Proteus netlist format generated from the schematic for the simulator (and the PCB module): a text listing of every part with its model/properties and every net with its pins, which can be written explicitly by Tools > Netlist Compiler (format SDF) or logged from a graph with 'Log netlist(s)'. Inspecting it shows exactly which model, pin mapping and property values the simulation used.
tools.usage: Tools > Netlist Compiler > Format SDF > Output to file/viewer; or Edit Graph > Log netlist(s) then view the Simulation Log
tools.example: Confirm that a vendor op-amp's X card lists the pins in the order given by SPICEPINS by reading the SDF.
tools.notes: SDF here is Labcenter's 'Schematic Description Format', unrelated to Standard Delay Format.

tools.name: Help menu (module help files, Getting Started guides, Help Center)
tools.description: Each module's Help menu opens its reference manual (Schematic Capture Help, PCB Layout Help, Proteus VSM Help, VSM Studio, Visual Designer, IoT Builder, EasyHDL, BOM, 3D Viewer, Gerber Viewer, Library Import) plus the Getting Started guides, the online Help Center/documentation and support links; the Home page links to tutorials, sample projects, the Labcenter YouTube channel and the community forums (support.labcenter.com/forums).
tools.usage: Help > <Module> Help (F1 in most dialogues opens context help); Help > About for version/licence details
tools.example: Help > Schematic Capture Help > 'Templates' chapter for the full list of Template-menu settings.
tools.notes: Email support (support@labcenter.com) answers within one to two working days; forums are community based.

tools.name: Proteus 8 vs Proteus 9 (framework and compatibility reference)
tools.description: Proteus 9 (first release 2024) replaced the 32-bit Proteus 8 shell with a native 64-bit, Unicode, platform-independent framework: light/dark themes, redesigned dialogues and object selectors, dockable widgets, three install modes, much faster live zone regeneration, the System Scope with live probes, dockable instruments, managed libraries, the Via Inspector and extended MicroPython support (9.0); EDAi ProPilot/ProTutor, Git/SVN libraries, silkscreen DRC and Visual Designer/IoT Builder for MicroPython (9.1); Measure and Move, Output Job Manager, micro-vias, object grouping, System Meter, BLE/RFID and STM32CubeIDE GDB debugging (9.2). Projects saved by 9 cannot be opened by 8; 8.15 already introduced a format break within 8.x.
tools.usage: Check Home page version; upgrade under the Update Service Contract; keep an 8.x copy for legacy .pdsprj if collaborators have not upgraded
tools.example: A team on 8.17 and 9.2 should standardise on one version before sharing edits, since 9.2 saves cannot be read by 8.17.
tools.notes: Feature-level differences between releases are documented on the labcenter.com 'What's new' pages per version.
